GeometryParadoxes
Game: Grey blobs seem to sit between rows of dark shapes, but nobody painted them there.
How to play: Slide the controls to change how many shapes you see and how big they are. Pick Rectangles or Circles, switch the colours, and move the dot with your mouse or arrow keys to look straight at a gap and watch its faint halo vanish.
4 50%
Look for the math

There are no grey spots in this picture. The old applet paints only a grid of dark shapes; the soft blobs you see between them are made by your eyes.

A grid of figures

The applet draws N × N figures in a square matrix, with N from 2 to 12. The size of each figure is round((min(width, height) − 20) × Part / 100 / N), where Part is the second slider (0 to 105). The space between neighbouring figure corners is rounded to a whole pixel too. Nothing in that formula mentions a blob.

How many gaps?

Between the figures there are (N − 1) × (N − 1) crossings of free background: nine when the applet starts with N = 4. The test checks every slider setting and confirms that all nine crossings stay open at Part = 50 on the applet's 360 × 440 canvas. At Part = 70 or more the figures touch or overlap and every crossing is covered. Rounding matters at the edges: on a short 400 × 300 canvas with 12 figures across, Part = 50 already closes the crossings.

Why the blob goes away

The page says a blob vanishes when you look straight at it, and this is an optical illusion of peripheral vision, not a change in the pixels. The gaze dot here lets you aim at a crossing: a faint halo marks the blob your eye supplies while you look off to one side, and it vanishes when you look straight at it. The grid itself never changes. The dot and halo are new; the Java applet had only two sliders, Rectangles/Circles, and Switch colors. The page calls the background white, while the applet's own default is light grey; this port uses the site's panel colour in both themes.

Try Part = 50 with 4 figures across, look away from a gap and then move the dot onto it. Then set Part = 75: the corridors close and there is nowhere for a blob to appear.
